title: Bach's Badinerie: The Baroque Dance Suite, Scoring and Binary Form
description: This lesson explores Bach's Badinerie from Orchestral Suite No. 2, covering the Baroque dance-suite tradition, its scoring for flute, strings and continuo, and its binary form structure.
content_html:
The Baroque Dance Suite

In the Baroque era (roughly 1600–1750), composers regularly wrote instrumental suites — collections of short movements based on the rhythms and character of fashionable court and social dances. Although the dances were originally meant for actual dancing, by Bach's time they had become stylised concert pieces: music that kept the dance's typical tempo, metre and mood but was written purely to be listened to.

A standard Baroque suite built its core around four dances: the allemande (a moderate German dance in four time), the courante (a running French dance in triple time), the sarabande (a slow, stately dance in triple time with weight on the second beat), and the gigue (a fast, lively dance, often in compound time). Composers frequently inserted extra, lighter ‘galanterie’ movements — such as minuets, gavottes and badinerie — between the sarabande and the closing gigue, giving audiences a change of pace and mood.

A Baroque suite is a set of contrasting dance-based movements, usually sharing the same key, designed for entertainment at court or in public concerts; each movement contrasts in tempo, metre and character while the whole suite hangs together tonally.

Bach's Orchestral Suite No. 2 and the Badinerie

Johann Sebastian Bach composed four orchestral suites, each written for a different combination of instruments. Orchestral Suite No. 2 in B minor, BWV 1067, is unique among the four because it features a solo flute as the leading melodic voice throughout, supported by strings and continuo. Scholars believe the suite may have originated during Bach's years in Cöthen (around 1717–1723) and was revised and performed again in Leipzig in the 1730s, where Bach directed a collegium musicum that gave regular public concerts.

The suite closes with the Badinerie, a French title meaning ‘playful jesting’ or ‘banter’. The name perfectly suits the movement's quick, light-hearted, teasing character. It has become one of Bach's most celebrated pieces, admired for its dazzling flute writing and its irrepressible energy, and it is frequently performed and studied on its own, separate from the rest of the suite.

Scoring: Flute, Strings and Continuo

The Badinerie is scored for solo transverse flute (the traverso, forerunner of the modern flute), a string section of first and second violins and violas, and continuo. The flute carries almost all of the melodic interest, its rapid, athletic lines standing out clearly above the accompanying strings, which mostly provide harmonic support, occasional imitative echoes, and rhythmic drive.

The continuo group, typically cello and harpsichord (sometimes with double bass doubling the cello line), supplies the bass line and fills out the harmony. The harpsichordist improvises chords above the written bass notes according to Baroque performance convention, giving the texture its characteristic busy, decorative harmonic support beneath the soaring flute part.

Continuo (or basso continuo) is the continuous bass line and harmonic accompaniment typical of Baroque music, usually played by a bass instrument such as cello alongside a chordal instrument such as harpsichord, which realises the harmony from the bass notes.

Binary Form Structure

Like most Baroque dance movements, the Badinerie is written in binary form: two contrasting sections, labelled A and B, each of which is repeated (giving the overall pattern AABB when performed). This repeated two-part structure was standard for dance movements of the period and gave both performers and dancers a clear, balanced shape to follow.

Section A begins in the tonic key of B minor and modulates during its course to the relative major, D major, ending there. Section B then begins in or near D major and works its way back through related keys to close firmly in the home key of B minor, giving the whole movement a satisfying sense of tonal departure and return.

Melodic and Rhythmic Character

The flute part is built from scalic runs, arpeggio-based figures and short melodic sequences (a musical idea repeated at a different pitch), all delivered in continuous semiquaver movement that demands real virtuosity from the performer. This constant motion, combined with a quick tempo, is what gives the Badinerie its restless, playful energy.

The texture is mostly homophony, with the flute's melody supported by the strings and continuo, though there are moments of imitation where the violins briefly echo or answer fragments of the flute's material, creating a sense of playful dialogue between the parts. Dynamics tend to be terraced, meaning they shift suddenly between louder and softer levels rather than gradually, which is typical of Baroque style since instruments of the period had limited capacity for gradual dynamic change.

Exam Focus: Key Features to Remember

For your listening exam, be ready to identify the Badinerie's key features: its origin as the closing galanterie movement of a Baroque dance suite, its scoring for solo flute with strings and continuo, its binary form with two repeated sections moving from B minor to the relative major and back, and its energetic, virtuosic semiquaver flute writing that reflects the playful meaning of its title.

Quick recall list: Bach, Orchestral Suite No. 2 in B minor BWV 1067; solo flute, strings and continuo; final movement of the suite; binary form (AABB); B minor to relative major D major and back; continuous semiquaver flute figuration; terraced dynamics; occasional imitation between flute and violins.
exam_tip_html: When asked to comment on the Badinerie's form, do not simply write ‘it is in binary form’ — examiners reward precision, so name the actual keys involved (for example, ‘Section A modulates from the tonic B minor to the relative major, D major, before Section B returns to B minor’); a common mistake is confusing binary form with ternary form because both have repeated sections, so always check whether the opening material returns unchanged at the end (ternary) or whether the piece simply moves between two different key areas without a full restatement of the very opening (binary).
conclusion_html: You should now be able to place the Badinerie within the Baroque dance-suite tradition, describe its scoring and binary form, and explain why its title suits its playful character — next, revisit the listening extracts and test yourself with the practice questions below before moving on to the second study-piece lesson.

practice_questions.text: State the meaning of the title 'Badinerie'.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark for 'playful jesting' or 'banter' or an equivalent accepted translation.

practice_questions.text: Name the solo instrument featured throughout Bach's Badinerie.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark for flute (traverso/transverse flute accepted).

practice_questions.text: Identify the form used in the Badinerie.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark for binary form (AABB accepted).

practice_questions.text: Describe the key scheme of the Badinerie's two sections.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark for Section A moving from B minor to relative major D major, 1 mark for Section B returning from D major/related keys back to B minor.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the scoring of Orchestral Suite No. 2 supports the character of the Badinerie.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for reference to solo flute carrying rapid virtuosic melodic lines (1), strings/continuo providing harmonic support and occasional imitation (1), and how this combination creates a light, playful, energetic effect matching the title (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how rhythm and texture combine to create the playful character of the Badinerie, referring to specific musical features.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks for detailed reference to continuous semiquaver movement, scalic/arpeggio figures and sequences, mostly homophonic texture with brief imitation between flute and violins, and terraced dynamics, linked clearly to the playful, energetic character.

flashcard_questions.a: A collection of contrasting stylised dance movements, usually sharing a key, written for entertainment at court or in concert.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'Badinerie' mean and where does it appear in Bach's suite?
flashcard_questions.a: It means playful jesting or banter, and it is the final movement of Bach's Orchestral Suite No. 2 in B minor, BWV 1067.
For solo flute with strings (violins and violas) and continuo (cello and harpsichord).

flashcard_questions.q: Describe the binary form key scheme of the Badinerie.
flashcard_questions.a: Section A moves from the tonic B minor to the relative major D major; Section B returns from D major/related keys back to B minor, both sections repeated.

flashcard_questions.q: What creates the playful character of the Badinerie's melody?
flashcard_questions.a: Continuous rapid semiquaver runs, scalic and arpeggio figures, and short melodic sequences played virtuosically by the flute.

glossary_terms.definition: A collection of contrasting instrumental movements, often based on dances, usually sharing the same key.
A French term meaning playful jesting or banter, used as the title of a light, energetic dance-style movement.
An optional lighter dance movement, such as a minuet, gavotte or badinerie, inserted into a Baroque suite alongside the standard four dances.
A musical structure in two contrasting sections, often each repeated, commonly used in Baroque dance movements.
The continuous bass line and harmonic accompaniment in Baroque music, typically played by a bass instrument and a chordal instrument such as harpsichord.
The home or main key of a piece of music, to which the harmony ultimately returns.
The major key that shares the same key signature as a given minor key, a third above the minor tonic.
A musical idea or melodic pattern repeated immediately at a higher or lower pitch.
A technique where one musical part copies or echoes material just played by another part.
Sudden shifts between louder and softer dynamic levels, without gradual crescendo or diminuendo, typical of Baroque music.
A texture in which a single melodic line is supported by accompanying harmony.
The Baroque transverse flute, forerunner of the modern flute, held sideways and played by blowing across a hole.
